Many have read Heidegger's remarks on our relations to things as saying that human beings are immersed in the world through language and everyday practices. This perspective suggests, on the one hand, that we cannot break through or extricate ourselves from our emplacement so as to get at things from the "outside," as it were, and, on the other hand, that the things of the world are never trumped by language or ideas. Our holistic entanglements are material and practical first and foremost. Hubert Dreyfus is a well-known proponent of this position and posits Heidegger as a "robust realist," meaning that Heidegger avoids the Scylla ofnaive realism and the Charybdis of idealism ("Coping" n.p.). The world is a participant in the ongoing event of human being-in-the-world, not a stage or backdrop to what human beings do and say. And this is a nuanced participation, with things emerging from and participating in human practices, and human practices in turn requiring things. Such an interpretation is fine as a first take, except that it exhibits a certain skewing: the nexus remains tethered to human being. Human usage and behavior become the privileged means of access to the background, and things, such as tools, light up to our awareness as we use them; then, when our attention shifts elsewhere, they dim back into the shadowy realm of equipment (Zeug) in general, the undifferentiated, always receding backdrop of"stuff."1 Heidegger certainly lends himself to such a reading. Speaking ofa room, he remarks that we encounter it not as a geometrical space but as "equipment for residingp that we have at least discovered, and that discovery and our activities yield

an arrangement that allows individual items to show themselves (BT 98). I take the steps downstairs into the basement, set out my books, organize my papers, boot the laptop, put some Klaus Schulze on the turntable, sit on the chair at the desk, insert the pen drive, enter words into the chapter file (i.e., write), read, take notes, edit, save the file, put on some Dexter Gordon. adjust the stereo volume, and so forth, with aspects of the room now near and now far from my attentions and activities. In various ways, these things all go together; there is an arrangement from which individual entities already derive their place wherefrom I can weave them through my activities. Entities in turn show up and dim back into the recesses as my attention flows variously through my purposeful activity.

In Tool-Being Graham Harman argues that such readings, reminiscent of Dreyfus, are not wrong but nevertheless miss something crucial to the nature of equipment and objects. Objects can no more be positioned solely within the horizon of human intention or awareness than language can. My example of the basement illustrates this tendency, since everything has its "nearness" and "farness" in relation to my attentions and intentions. One could of course add more history here and pile on thick description across the attentions and intentions of other people, social roles, and equipment. But none of this suffices to give us any ultimate grip on the object. Harman argues that "ifwe could total up all the 'contexts, roles, and social goals' in which a specific bridge or flagpole are currently embedded, this would still not give us the being of these objects" (TB 124). Any use or meaning that I or anyone else can bring, or even the plenitude of people, uses, contexts, histories, and other objects that could be brought forward, only serves to present some particular qualities out of the object's fulsomeness, or what Harman calls its "grand, dark abundance" (TB 125). Indeed. as the new wave of cognitive science (such as the work of Andy Clark, Paul Dourish, Anthony Chemero, and so on) demonstrates, the use of tools and local environmental scaffolding inspires changes in our sense of embodiment, blurring boundaries; to use a computer mouse, for instance, amounts to making that mouse part of one's body, and in so doing, it effectively disappears.8 Thus, predicating ontological distinctions on human attention and its shifting cognitive and bodily boundaries is fruitless; the ontological has to manifest beyond such human-derived loci, and thus withdrawal does not depend on human perception or any other singular interaction.

In short, Harman seeks above all to provide an ontology that casts the withdrawal of objects in realist terms, making it transcend any direct perception, and in so doing to transform what realism can be. In our activities

Dwelling, then, entails more than existing and subsisting; it extends beyond simply doing what we need to do-working, socializing, building-to survive to include the richness that is developed and pursued in how we are doing so. Building is not just construction, notjust technics. Nor is it isolable, except at cost, from ambient concerns. To understand place in terms of building necessitates the fullest possible understanding of what makes a location a location. As Heidegger goes on to explain, the fourfold is already wrought with the building of the farmhouse, since the building ofit, which sprang from dwelling, is already a located response to and a living with the fourfold. The farmhouse is built from and sustained by what the earth gives

and lies nestled in the earth's hollows; it receives its direction and temporality from the sky and is further sustained by what the sky brings; the divinities are traced in thankfulness and respect, fear and hope; and death and birth and all the cares of mortals are knit into the house and responsive to the other three aspects of the fourfold, as each of the others similarly join together. None of these things is present in any simple and direct manner. but they can all be seen as gathered in the way of life that gave rise to the farmhouse. Thus, the fourfold cannot be reduced to direct presence, as it is also what remains concealed, although we too often take the mundane persistence of presence as all there is, since it is most near to our everyday concerns. Place is never given in its entirety.

But here we come to the crucial point. This withdrawing is also a form of supporting; it is the repletion of all that is, which in turn ensures that the world is always more than what we make ofit. If the world is to make claims ,on us, ifwe are to dwell in such manner as to attune ourselves to what is noninstrumental. nonrepresentational, then this withdrawal becomes es- :sential. In other words, human knowledge is al ways only partial, and rather tha1\ see this as an invitation to extend knowledge further, as ifwe could pry open all mystery and have it stand revealed before us, Heidegger argues that what remains unconcealed is itself valuable. Dwelling makes being's concealment an occasion for joy and humbleness, thought and insight, guidance and action. It grants the world a kind of meaning or value that, while it cannot speak directly (and hence is neither meaning nor value, exactly), nevertheless calls us in its holding sway and conditions every aspect of our being together. This is the productive "acknowledgment of what is not human in the context of what is" (Thiele, Timely 179). Thus, a location is inseparable from its unique expanse and its ecological connectedness to larger surroundings; all take part in making place a place. Human building arises from place, of course, and is a further disclosure of place, but Heidegger seems to indicate that there is something sound and hale in attuning ourselves to place's role in our constructive pursuits rather than seeking only human-derived, technical, or efficiency-driven projects. I will explore this idea further in the next chapter.

Taylor's book, for which this digression on authoring is a performative microcosm, usefully introduces complexity theory, or, more specifically, theories concerning the behavior and impact of complex adaptive systems, and considers the implications of these theories for the humanities. Of special interest is the emphasis on complexity's relation to network culture. Network culture is complex in an emergent and ecological sense. It is important to underscore that a complex system is distinguished from a complicated one by the process of emergence: in the usage I deploy here, something complicated can be disassembled into its component parts, no matter how intricate, while something complex cannot be adequately analyzed through or predicted from the component elements but rather enters a new state of order or equilibrium that transcends the initial state (Cilliers viii-ix). An airplane is complicated; a pond ecosystem or the brain is complex. While Cilliers's example is overly simple, since an airplane must be involved in complex processes, too (aspects of wear and tear, metal fatigue, and so on may well be better understood as complex), the main point remains. Complexity evolves; it is dynamic, and hence, while equilibrium can result, such stability is an achievement with the conditions for its transformation already built in. Such equilibrium, in other words, is tempor ary, or a perspectival view that masks how the system is already far from equilibrium, just in ways not perhaps apparent. Hence the importance, for Taylor, of bringing contemporary network culture into conversation with theories of complexity. By increasing the number of variables in circulation, including the spectr al/virtual, network culture pushes us toward acknowledging complexity in ways that modernist theory and modernist culture simultaneously prepared us to see and found ways and reasons to resist.Network cultur e cannot be so forestalled, as Taylor sees it; we are confronted with

and haunted not only by increasing points of connection but also by their interactive emergence into new forms. Digitality provides new haunts, new places for the spectral traces and strands of communication, figuration, and affect to circulate. Networks, digital and otherwise, become dynamically and unpredictably complex, and in this chapter I consider how networks and complexity can augment a theory of ambient rhetoric. Thus, in many respects, this chapter takes up earlier essays in the field that first broached issues of complexity, such as those by Louise Weatherbee Phelps, Marilyn Cooper, and Richard Lanham, scholars who all saw, surprisingly early, complexity's importance for rhetoric and composition.

In this chapter I will first attempt to bring my previous discussion of ambient rhetoric, including my observations on the chora and kairos, into discussion with the theories and idioms of complexity theory so as to continue reworking these terms in line with important scientific insights. I do this not to value one field over the other but to argue implicitly for the benefits of putting them in conversation. 2 I will then seek to illuminate the practicality of ambient rhetoric by showing some concrete examples of ambience and thereby also point to limitations with the concept of the network. I will next begin making some connections to Heidegger that foreshadow later, more extended discussions of his work; here I begin to show how his thought helps us reconceptualize context as including human being, or better, as participating in human being. One way to do this is to reconsider the meaning of the early Heidegger's locution das Situations-Ich, the situational-I, or as might be preferable given its network culture allusion, the I-situation (or iSituation).3 This term was the precursor to Heidegger's later and more famous locution for human being, Dasein (being there) (Kisiel 64). "I-situation" is useful precisely because it still retains a sense ofI-ness and hence can provide an entryway for more intensely thinking the dissolution of any traditional notion of the subject, such as the dissolution reflected in the idea that kairos wills a situation. Lastly, I will again bring a new materialist perspective into the conversation, which Taylor, too, attempts to do via his notion ofincarnation, though with only varying degrees of success.

(Haunted) Houses in Motion: Networks as a Principle of Being

Jeff Rice describes this last point well when he states, "The best demonstration of choral moves on the Web can be seen (but not only found) in the hypertextual link that allows writers the capability of developing threads around single words or ideas, and that requires readers to navigate these threads in various ways. The link is indicative of a new media push to reorganize space in terms of meaning construction" (Rhetoric 35). Note Rice's observation that choric invention involves more than just finding, since it attends to a reorganization of space, meaning that invention is integrated into the process of finding itself; there is, then, no simple "finding" exterior to the ambient media environment. And as Vitanza remarks, such new media writing, or electracy, as Ulmer often calls it, is choric in that it too is a third kind, following but being neither progress from nor a hybrid of orality and literacy ("Writing" n.p.). In other words, there is no need to reach to a Hegelian narrative of sublation to understand choric writing. Indeed, it might be better to say that rhetorical invention has always been choric, that topic writing was simply the way choric writing has predominately been disclosed to us, and that new technologies have afforded us fresh perspectives on invention that resonate strongly with the ch6ra. Topic writing is not abandoned, then; it is inhabited differently. But this also means that choric invention is itself ubiquitous; a book, a web text, a classroom, and a viral video making the Internet rounds would all have their choric bearing.

If choric writing is ubiquitous-ambient, as it were-then the stakes in adopting it lie not in demonstrating the "reality" of what is in fact everyday activity but in garnering the ability to bring it to rhetorical theory or finding

in such practices fresh rhetorical opportunities. In this respect, the chora allows Ulmer to reconceive the relations between a writer and his or her "specific position in the time and space of a culture" (Heuretics 33). This is not solely a matter of the hermeneutics of cultural identity, except insofar as they are extended to a broader project of generating texts appropriate for the electronic age and the question of how an inventio suited to such generation can be formulated. Hawk describes this as using "the function of location to map your specific position in time, place, and culture and invent a heuretic in the process" (Counter-History 240). Ulmer's chora moves us from thinking that is "linear indexical" to a form that is "network associational" (Heuretics 36) and is concerned less with logic than with memory (experience, both personal and externalized/stored) and intuition (37), less with verification than with learning (xii). The radical expansion and externalization of memory in cultural discourses, electronic networks, and databases creates an ocean of information that in turn requires navigation (30). One must be careful on this point, however. As suggested previously by both Kristeva and Derrida, the chora is precariously placed in regard to reasoning and discourse, meaning that it stretches our prior and rather entrenched sense of what these things might be. Ulmer observes that by providing new equipment of memory, computers also transform people and institutions (36). Choric navigation, then, moves us toward a reconceptualization or a fresh disclosure of place accompanied by a further refinement of what it means to navigate, associate, and compose. For Ulmer, this will mean, among other things, that a hypermedia composer constructs not arguments per se but an "information environment" through which a user will choose a path. Such a notion of place, and the kinds of activities that emerge from it, are properly understood as dispersed or distributed. As Rice's previously cited observation indicates, this is precisely why the hyper link has such inventive capacity, since it enacts distribution.

But given the centrality of place in these discussions, I want to further emphasize that these rhetorical forms rely on processes of externalization and dispersion. Encoding word and image in the electronic media involves an externalization, to be sure, and Ulmer takes time to develop these ideas in detail. But such processes accentuate an ongoing attunement to the materialities of body, place, and environment that have been picked up in numerous disciplines at this time, including the sciences. This moves me toward some final remarks. Dwelling on Toronto Island discloses the environment as a complex relational stitchwork of things individuating themselves, emerging from the as-a-whole into mutually conditioning and supporting aspects of being, including the human. The island is not nature. It is not separate from the human and hence in need of preservation from the ravages of human work and technology. Rather, the island is integral to the unique character of dwelling there. What Princen and the Toronto Islanders dance around, partially disclosing and not quite articulating, is that as a place that emerges through dwelling, the island gathers and is gathered by the fourfold. This occasions the strength of the residents' decades-long resistance to city planning and the lure of comfort and money. This is where the rejection of automobility emerges and draws its vigor. This is why the rejection is neither negative nor reactionary: it is the power of affirmation nourished in the "as a whole" of island life. My point is not that humans assign the values that some call "uses" but rather that the mutual conditioning of earth, sky, divinities, and mortals brings a haleness (which cannot be confused with utopian dreams, lack of struggle, etc., in some sort of easy holistic harmony) to "their" way of being, where "their" extends beyond mortals to include nonhuman elements.

This view offers a still greater understanding of the deficiency in Latour's discussion of the parliament of things. Latour's remarks suggest that addressing the Toronto Island conflict would be a mat ter of bringing all the elements of the island, considered as an assemblage of human and nonhuman actants, to political representation and deliberation. Such elements would include, presumably, the land, beaches, plants, animals, roads,

buildings, and everything else. Nor would Latour limit the considerations to distributed representation for things, for he extends the range of forums for interacting with things beyond the political to include religion, public discourse, the arts, science, and more. This remains an important point, since it grants value to disparate ways of dealing with things of concern. But Latour is less able to attend to the conditions of possibility for remaking the political into Dingpolitik. Everything is as it is, available for assembly and reassembly but still already there. Political assembly becomes a matter of human willing and pursuit, with the forums ready-made and rhetoric conceived as persuasion in its traditional sense, except that it now includes nonhuman actants and acknowledges their agency.

Heidegger's insights remain more profound. His rejoinder to Latour would be that such political will and the rhetorics required to enact it ultimately reinforce the priority of the human. There is no fundamental tempering of the notion of will itself as it emerges in the assemblage and hence as it underpins Latour's conception ofrhetoric and politics; there are only the complications resulting from the establishment of nonhuman intermediaries. Reconceiving nonhumans as agents affecting even humans constitutes an advance, but Latour offers no larger sense of the "as a whole" within which humans, as well as everything else, find relation and place and that constitutes the possibility for everything's being what it is and for our being as we are. The examples Princen offers, including the Toronto Islanders as well as various European cities that have closed their downtown areas to autos, are remarkable because in each case, a way oflife enacts an attunement to this profound conditionality. 13 The important point here is that a Dingpolitik does not come first, opening up and transforming our existing political practices by an inclusive fiat extended to nonhumans. Rather, dwelling as attunement to this conditionality, disclosed in and through the fourfold, already gives rise to what can emerge as Dingpolitik.

For this reason, I prefer the metaphor of the ambient. What is ambient is immersive, osmotic, peripheral. Ambience is not so link driven, for it suggests many tactile forms besides connections among already established points or nodes. The link gives us little leeway with the more ephemeral, nuratic modalities of everyday life. Indeed, the network is ultimately still invested in binaries (movement and node, line and point), even if such binaries are wrenched by the strange loops of emergent behavior. The richly osmotic character of ambience includes choric engagement and interaction beyond the link. As I will address in the next chapter, this includes affect: affect certainly circulates in and gives rise to networks, but we need to augment this understanding of affect as more fundamental, being the mood, or affective comportment, from which our attitudes, decisions, and actions emerge. The attunement to what is choric reminds us that we cannot reduce the world to simple presence, to what is already revealed. but must rather attend to genesis, how things come to be as they are. The concept of ambience is better suited to gathering kairos and logos into a worldliness that includes but also transcends the human, showing how they take part in us even as they will us, speak us.

But how, exactly, do kairos and logos pick out various ways in which discourse and environs come to speak or will us? What can show this to be something other than a return to the subject/object split, which privileges

an objective, exterior environment over a subject? As I have previously argued. subject and object derive from an originary belongingness, and if we want to keep these terms, we need to see them more as a "mutual taking part in." But insofar as this "taking part in" is ultimately ambient, it simultaneously includes and exceeds the "subject"; only in this sense can we understand the kairotic environs as willing us. Nor, as should become clear, am I merely collapsing distinct realms into an abstract unity; this is equally impossible, for the ambient, if thought alongside complexity theory, can be seen as an emergent level of order discontinuous from what is given by the ensemble of original individual elements. Rather than possess some a priori ontological status, distinctions emerge dynamically and fluidly within the situation and are ultimately only an additional modality in the overall ambience. As I began this chapter with Taylor's meditation on a writer writing, I want to once again consider what happens as a writer writes. But I begin doing so by going back before Taylor.

Barrett J. Mandel's 1980 essay "The Writer Writing Is Not at Home" stands as remarkably prescient for my purposes, and it makes an illuminating contrast with Taylor's work. Mandel opens his essay with a snippet from an interview with the American painter Jasper Johns, conducted, oddly enough, by Michael Crichton:

The author [Crichton] asks Johns why he has just made a change in the handle of a spoon in a lithograph on which he is working. Johns answers, "Because I did." The author asks, "But what did you see?" Johns: '·I saw that it should be changed." Author: "Well, if you changed it, what was wrong with it before?" Johns: "Nothing. I tend to think one thing is as good as another." Author: "Then why change it?" Johns, after a sigh and a pause: "Well, I may change it again." Author: "Why?" Johns: "Well, I won't know until I doit." (370)

This is high comedy, no doubt, with Crichton coming off as a clueless interviewer. 19 Still, Mandel notes the difficulties in communication and defends Johns as being as honest as he can. The artist, Mandel argues, creates "out ofno prior knowledge, thought, plan, or expectations" (370). Plans and thoughts do come into play, but "the work of art does not arise from them; they do not cause the work of art to materialize" (370). In short, like everything else, dwelling resists any reduction to forms of simple presence, in this case, to directly available and revealed best practices for homemaking. If we were always already at home, if home were never at issue (never a "thing" for us), then homemaking would not be challenging for us; ultimately it can never be fully realized. Dwelling is an ongoing and never stilled process ofattunement, disclosure, and building. Thus, dwelling is rhetorical in an ambient sense: disclosure and attunement emerge out of a worldly affectability, so that dwelling's coming to manifestation is a matter of ongoing differentiation. In what follows, I will try to elaborate on this point more plainly; specifically, I will try to rethink stability in an ambient key, arguing that it is less a cessation of movement or change than a way of dwelling attuned to sustainability and achieved through the lived realization of sufficiency.

Dwelling in/as Sufficiency

Bringing Heidegger's concept of dwelling into ongoing struggles with sustainability, particularly regarding the automobile, does not just show but performs how humans become cognizant of and organize their practices around what in contemporary environmental discourse we would call an ecology, or things and forces joined together in dynamic coexistence sustainable over time. The English word ecology, which derives from the German Okologie, coined by the biologist Ernst Haeckel in 1866, stems from the ancient Greek word oikos, meaning "house," "home," or "dwelling." Haeckel drew on oikos to bring home the sense of ecology as a comprehensive science of an organism's relation to its environment,

with environment here being where one dwells (Thiele.Indra's 3). As I have shown, when Heidegger discusses dwelling, he describes the relation not only as one of directly co-responding but as one of hearkening to directives or being conditioned by things; for Heidegger, that is, ecology entails more than presence. Ecological literature, however, often describes ecologies in (sometimes overly) holistic terms focused on the powerful role of the feedback loops that emerge within circulating, sustaining activities and material interactions. Feedback loops supply necessary encouragement and constraint allowing for the dynamic self-organization characteristic of a flourishing ecology; this can even be attributed to a direct sense of a "natural" law that we must acknowledge or follow.• Regulatory mechanisms and their "values" are in a sense "built in" to an ecological system. Thus ecologies are often characterized in terms of efficiency, since they tend to reward the maximization of potential. At the same time. ecologies curtail or otherwise redirect efficiency so that nothing gets too far out of balance; if it does, the ecology "self-corrects," adapts, morphs, or fails in accordance with autopoesis, or self-organization (Maturana and Varela, 47-52; Varela, Thompson, and Rosch 88-91: Hayles 136). In short, while efficiency certainly constitutes a vector for an ecology, the notion relevant here can significantly differ from the kind of abstracted and totalized notion of efficiency common to instrumentalized technological thinking,5Efficiency matters because an ecology is at every moment entangled in constraining forces-checks and balances, if you will-necessary for a sustainable trajectory. Insofar as efficiency is thus always tempered, we might better consider it an example of sufficiency. In a sustainable ecological system, efficiency emerges as forms of sufficiency (Thiele, Timely 179).

What is at stake in this qualification of efficiency? We might keep in mind the general definition of efficiency: maximum yield for minimum effort, a point that resonates with Heidegger's arguments about technological enframing insofar as both can be conceived as forms of ordering (QCT 8, 15)_ More precisely, technology already conditions how efficiency is conceived and I ived. This occurs not deterministically but rather ontologically. in shaping how worldly affordances reveal themselves as what they are, for technology is a way of revealing the world, or more pointedly, a revealing that challenges (herausfordern) the world as a standing reserve (Bestand), a stockpile of resources to be exploited (QCT 17). Empedocles and Heidegger continually emphasized the need to forge a positive way forward, to work not just with who people are but with where they are. We cannot escape the infrastructures, industries, and lifeways people currently have but must work within and through them towards a more ecologically attuned dwelling. In this regard, science, technology, and capitalism will need to become part of that path, despite the fact that these are some of the most common targets for environmentalist critique. On these points I take inspiration from Peter Sloterdijk's digression on spaceships in his massive philosophical trilogy, Spheres. Sloterdijk argues that spaceships are more than technological objects—they are equally ontological interventions. The suturing

of a thing to ontology harkens back to Heidegger, and we can see how Sloterdijk's spaceship updates Heidegger's jugs and bridges. But there is also an inversion: jugs and bridges evoke an interconnected whole to which we are all wedded and indebted; a spaceship, however, operates in a realm of extreme inhospitality. Space is nonconductive for nearly all life as we know it. Since no aspect of dwelling in space can be taken for granted, a spaceship "constitutes a world model," a kind of "immanence machine."73 The level of explicatory detail necessary for surviving in such a harsh environment is vertiginous. To give one small example: astronauts must sleep with fans next to them, less their exhalations, which do not move in zero gravity, suffocate them in a bubble of nitrogen and carbon dioxide.74 There is no resting on unexplicated assumptions, as is possible back on Earth where the ecological background can simply be assumed, as Moore exemplifed through capitalism's cavalier appropriations of nature. Space lacks such "ontological comfort."75

The point, Sloterdijk argues, is that "space travel amounts to an ontological alphabetization: what follows from it is that the elements of being-in-the-world can, and must, be written."76 Sloterdijk picks up the thread we saw connecting Empedocles and Aristotle in the movement from roots to elements, where increasing abstraction and alphabetization formalize as science and episteme. Sloterdijk also counters Abram's argument that abstraction goes hand in hand with the West's loss of intimacy with the environment. Rather, Sloterdijk taps a great affrmation resonant with Empedocles and Heidegger. It is the affrmation of the fourfold. The lesson is that abstraction and alphabetization also gather the fourfold and disclose the worldly depths of rich interconnection. Spaceships necessitate this insight. For life to maintain itself in space, bubbles of lifeworld must be constructed. To construct a bubble of lifeworld requires a profoundly rich explication of an ecological background we take for granted on earth, where our lifeworld is simply given. For spacecraft, these ABCs of lifeworlding must be spelled out and implemented through the technics of disclosure and building. As Heidegger has argued, to build is to dwell, and here we see how this manifests in even the most focused technological enterprise.77

The explicative disclosure necessary for space travel thus affrms some of environmentalism's biggest demons—abstraction, science, technology, capitalist progress. But this disclosive work pushes through their dangers and lights up their roles in the ecological lifeworld it is claimed they despoil. Still, it may be argued that space travel is a feeting pursuit
